text.p: Singapore on Monday began the final countdown to general elections which the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) is expected to win in a romp.
President Ong Teng Cheong dissolved parliament and the government set December 23 as the date for nomination of candidates.
The moves pointed to an election day in the week ending January 4, political analysts said.
According to election rules, the campaign has to be a minimum nine days long but can last up to eight weeks. In previous elections, the PAP, which has won them all, has opted for the minimum.
Elections have usually taken place on a Saturday.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has kept the country guessing for weeks over when he would call the elections, which must be held by April.

But over the weekend he gave the strongest clue yet that the elections would be held sooner rather than later, saying he expected to decide dates after "smelling the air" in an opposition-held constituency on Sunday.
Former prime minister Lee Kwan Yew said at the weekend that the polls would be held in the next few weeks.
In the last elections in 1991, Goh's PAP, which has won every election since 1959, won all but four of the 81 elected seats in parliament.

Political analysts said the most closely watched aspect of the polls would be the percentage of the vote won by the PAP, whose share slipped to 61 percent in the last elections from 63.2 percent in 1988.
Veteran opposition leader J.B. Jeyaretnam, head of the Workers Party, told Reuters he expected the PAP to retain power.
"I think we should increase the number of seats" won by the opposition," he added. "We are as ready as we can be."
Opposition parties say they expect to put up about 40 candidates this time and hope to win at least 10 seats in what will be a parliament of 83 elected members.
They advocate a kinder, gentler government than that provided by the firm hand of the PAP.

However, the PAP argues that its style of government has brought huge wealth to Singapore, where per capita gross domestic product is higher than in former colonial power Britain, and influence beyond its size.
